The other modules in this repository count injuries and deaths that someone recorded. Most
work-related deaths are never recorded as work-related: they are deaths from heart disease,
stroke, lung disease and cancer, years after the exposure. The **WHO/ILO Joint Estimates**
estimate this hidden burden for 183 countries.

For each **pair** of an occupational risk factor and a disease (for example *asbestos* and
*mesothelioma*), WHO and the ILO estimate the share of all cases of the disease that would not
have happened without the exposure at work: the **population attributable fraction (PAF)**.
Multiplying the PAF by the total number of deaths from the disease gives the deaths
**attributable** to work. The same is done for **DALYs** (disability-adjusted life years): years
of healthy life lost through early death or disability.

Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/intl-who-ilo-joint-estimates/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), .default = col_guess()))
}

burden <- read_tidy("burden_global_regional.csv.gz")   # global and WHO regions, by age
countries <- read_tidy("burden_country.csv.gz")         # 183 countries, ages 15+
exposure <- read_tidy("exposure.csv.gz")               # people exposed (2 risk factors)
disease_rate <- read_tidy("disease_death_rate.csv.gz") # deaths from all work-related diseases

# The solar UV estimates were added in 2023; leave them out to match the 2021 report totals
uv <- "Occupational exposure to solar ultraviolet radiation"

# Shorter risk factor names for plots
short_risk <- function(x) str_remove(x, "^Occupational (exposure to )?|^Exposure to ")

global_2016 <- burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", year == 2016)
```

# Part 1. How many people die from their work?

```{r totals}
global_2016 |>
  filter(risk_factor != uv) |>
  group_by(measure) |>
  summarise(total = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE))

by_risk <- global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths") |>
  group_by(risk_factor) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths[risk_factor != uv])) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
by_risk

by_risk |>
  filter(deaths > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(deaths, fct_reorder(short_risk(risk_factor), deaths))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Deaths attributable to occupational risk factors, world, 2016",
       x = "Deaths", y = NULL)
```

# Part 2. Diseases versus injuries

```{r outcomes}
global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths", risk_factor != uv) |>
  mutate(type = if_else(risk_factor == "Occupational injuries", "Injury", "Disease")) |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths))

global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths") |>
  group_by(cause) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths)) |>
  head(10)
```

# Part 3. Trends from 2000 to 2016

```{r trends}
burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", measure == "deaths",
         year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2016)) |>
  group_by(risk_factor, year) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(deaths > 10000) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, deaths, colour = short_risk(risk_factor))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths by risk factor", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", colour = NULL)

exposure |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years",
         risk_factor == "Exposure to long working hours") |>
  select(year, people_exposed = number, percent_of_population_15plus = percent)
```

```{r regions-sex}

global_2016_by_sex |>

global_2016_by_sex |>

  ggplot(aes(deaths, fct_reorder(short_risk(risk_factor), deaths), fill = sex)) +
```

# Part 5. Age

```{r age}
burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", year == 2016, measure == "deaths",
         age_group != "15+ years", risk_factor != uv) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(risk_factor == "Occupational injuries", "Injuries", "Diseases"),
```

# Part 6. Comparing countries

Rates here are per 100,000 people aged 15 and over (the whole working-age population, not only
workers). Rates of different pairs for the same population can be added.

```{r countries}
compare <- c("United States of America", "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland",
             "Australia", "India", "China", "Brazil", "Nigeria", "Germany")

country_rates <- countries |>
  filter(year == 2016, sex == "Both", measure == "deaths", risk_factor != uv) |>
  mutate(group = case_when(risk_factor == "Occupational injuries" ~ "injuries",
                           risk_factor == "Exposure to long working hours" ~ "long_hours",
                           TRUE ~ "other_diseases")) |>
  group_by(country, group) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = rate) |>
  mutate(total = injuries + long_hours + other_diseases)

filter(country_rates, country %in% compare) |> arrange(desc(total))

ggplot(country_rates, aes(total)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Work-related death rate, 183 countries, 2016",
       x = "Deaths per 100,000 population aged 15+", y = "Countries")
```

**Questions**

   denominator (population versus workers), which deaths are included, and modelling versus counting.
2. In high-income countries, what share of the total work-related death rate is from disease?
3. Which countries have the highest total rates? What do they have in common?

# Part 7. Population attributable fractions and uncertainty

The PAF for a single exposure with prevalence *p* and relative risk *RR* is

PAF = p (RR - 1) / (p (RR - 1) + 1)

The WHO/ILO systematic reviews found that working 55 or more hours a week raises the risk of
stroke by about 35% (RR = 1.35; Descatha et al., 2020) and of ischaemic heart disease by about
17% (RR = 1.17; Li et al., 2020), compared with working 35 to 40 hours. Both reviews are in
*Environment International*.

```{r paf}
p_long_hours <- exposure |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", year == 2016,
         risk_factor == "Exposure to long working hours") |>
  pull(percent) / 100

paf <- function(p, rr) p * (rr - 1) / (p * (rr - 1) + 1)
tibble(cause = c("Stroke", "Ischaemic heart disease"), rr = c(1.35, 1.17)) |>
  mutate(prevalence = p_long_hours, simple_paf = paf(prevalence, rr))

# Uncertainty: width of the 95% uncertainty interval relative to the estimate
global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths", number > 1000) |>
  mutate(relative_width = (number_upper - number_lower) / number) |>
  select(risk_factor, cause, number, number_lower, number_upper, relative_width) |>
  arrange(desc(relative_width))
```

**Questions**

1. Your simple PAF for stroke is smaller than the PAF in the WHO/ILO report (6.9% of stroke
   deaths in 2016). WHO applied the exposure by age and sex, and with a time lag (exposure years
   earlier causes disease now). Explain why each of these could make the PAF larger.
2. Which estimates are the most uncertain? Why might the uncertainty interval still be too narrow
   (what sources of error does it not include)?
3. A PAF answers the question "how many deaths would be prevented if nobody had been exposed?"
   Is that a realistic target for prevention? What would you report to a policy maker instead?

# Part 8. What is not included

The Joint Estimates cover 41 pairs of risk factor and disease (plus solar UV and skin cancer,
added in 2023). Many known occupational hazards are not included.

**Questions**
